Farms That Grow Upwards

As cities grow and farmland becomes scarcer, some engineers and farmers are looking up rather than out. Vertical farms grow crops indoors, in stacked layers that can rise many metres high. Instead of sunlight, the plants receive light from LED lamps, and instead of soil, their roots often sit in water that contains carefully measured nutrients.

Supporters point to several advantages. Because the environment is fully controlled, crops can be harvested all year round regardless of the weather. Water is recycled within the system, so these farms typically use far less of it than traditional fields. Since insects are kept out, pesticides are rarely needed. And when a farm is built inside a city, vegetables can reach shops within hours rather than days, which reduces transport costs and keeps the food fresher.

Critics, however, are less enthusiastic. Lighting and climate control consume enormous amounts of electricity, and unless that energy comes from renewable sources, the environmental benefits may be smaller than they first appear. Building costs are also high, which is why most vertical farms focus on fast-growing, valuable crops such as lettuce and herbs. Staple foods like wheat or rice, which need a lot of space and time, are still far more practical to grow in open fields.

For now, then, vertical farming seems unlikely to replace traditional agriculture. A more realistic role may be to complement it, supplying cities with fresh greens while conventional farms continue to feed the world.

quizzes.passage:
In Defence of Boredom

We live in an age in which boredom has become almost impossible. The moment we have to wait — for a bus, in a queue, for a kettle to boil — most of us reach for our phones. It seems harmless: why sit doing nothing when there are messages to read and videos to watch? Yet a growing number of psychologists suggest that by eliminating boredom, we may be losing something valuable.

Boredom, they argue, is not simply an unpleasant emptiness. It is a signal that our current situation is not satisfying us, and it pushes us to look for something more meaningful. When the mind has nothing external to focus on, it begins to wander, connecting memories, ideas and plans in unexpected ways. Many people report that their best ideas arrive in the shower or on a long walk — precisely the moments when they are not being entertained.

This does not mean that every dull moment leads to brilliance. Chronic boredom, especially when people feel trapped in situations they cannot change, is linked to frustration and low mood. The difference seems to lie in how we respond. Boredom that we escape from instantly teaches us nothing; boredom that we tolerate for a while can become the starting point for curiosity and creativity.

Perhaps, then, the next time you are waiting for a bus, it is worth leaving the phone in your pocket. You may simply be bored for ten minutes — or you may have your next good idea.

In Defence of Boredom

We live in an age in which boredom has become almost impossible. The moment we have to wait — for a bus, in a queue, for a kettle to boil — most of us reach for our phones. It seems harmless: why sit doing nothing when there are messages to read and videos to watch? Yet a growing number of psychologists suggest that by eliminating boredom, we may be losing something valuable.

Boredom, they argue, is not simply an unpleasant emptiness. It is a signal that our current situation is not satisfying us, and it pushes us to look for something more meaningful. When the mind has nothing external to focus on, it begins to wander, connecting memories, ideas and plans in unexpected ways. Many people report that their best ideas arrive in the shower or on a long walk — precisely the moments when they are not being entertained.

This does not mean that every dull moment leads to brilliance. Chronic boredom, especially when people feel trapped in situations they cannot change, is linked to frustration and low mood. The difference seems to lie in how we respond. Boredom that we escape from instantly teaches us nothing; boredom that we tolerate for a while can become the starting point for curiosity and creativity.

Perhaps, then, the next time you are waiting for a bus, it is worth leaving the phone in your pocket. You may simply be bored for ten minutes — or you may have your next good idea.

quizzes.passage:
The Last Keeper

For thirty-two years, Ilyas had climbed the hundred and twelve steps of the lighthouse every evening to light the lamp. He knew every crack in the stone walls and every change in the sound of the sea. Ships passing the dangerous rocks below had never seen him, but many of their sailors owed him their lives.

The letter arrived on a grey morning in March. The lighthouse was to be automated: a computer in a city office would now control the lamp, and a keeper would no longer be needed. Ilyas read the letter twice, folded it carefully and placed it under the clock on the kitchen table, where it stayed for a week.

On his last evening, he climbed the steps more slowly than usual. At the top, he did not light the lamp; it lit itself at exactly the programmed minute. For a moment he felt useless, like an old tool left on a shelf. Then he noticed a small fishing boat struggling against the wind near the rocks. Out of habit, he picked up the radio and guided the fisherman to the safe channel, calmly, step by step, as he had done a hundred times before.

When the boat was safe, the fisherman's voice came through the radio: 'Thank you, whoever you are.' Ilyas smiled. Machines, he thought, could light a lamp. But they could not hear fear in a man's voice. He went down the steps for the last time, feeling, for the first time in weeks, that his work had mattered.
